# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations, but they differ in their approach to data ownership, scalability, and cost. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Slack to Element, particularly those who value data ownership and are looking for a self-hosted solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user per month.
* Data Ownership: Element allows teams to own and control their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, but requires more resources and expertise to manage, while Slack handles scalability automatically.
* Feature Difference: Element offers end-to-end encryption, while Slack does not offer this feature by default.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good customer support
* Scalable and reliable
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* End-to-end encryption
* Highly customizable
* Data ownership and control
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams who value ease of use and don't mind paying for a scalable and reliable solution. It's particularly well-suited for small to medium-sized teams who don't have the technical expertise to manage a self-hosted solution. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution. This is particularly well-suited for large teams or organizations with strict data security requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure your Element instance to match your Slack setup, including integrations and customizations.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's scalability requires careful planning and management to ensure reliable performance. However, for teams who value data ownership and control, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element if you have a large team, strict data security requirements, and the technical expertise to manage a self-hosted solution.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) who value data ownership and control
* Teams with strict data security requirements
* Organizations with the technical expertise to manage a self-hosted solution
* Teams who don't need Slack's proprietary features
* Teams who are looking for a free and self-hosted solution

## FAQ
### Is Element free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted. However, you will need to pay for server costs and maintenance.
### Can I use Element with a small team?
Yes, but it may not be the best choice, as Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
### Is Element scalable?
Yes, but it requires careful planning and management to ensure reliable performance.
### Can I import my Slack data into Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption and allows teams to own and control their data.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for team collaboration, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, possibly due to concerns over data ownership or costs. The core use case for both tools is to facilitate team communication and collaboration, and someone might switch to gain more control over their data or reduce expenses.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to self-host and maintain full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more straightforward onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless issue tracking and project management, whereas Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Strong mobile app support
* Robust customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible through plugins
* Strong focus on security and compliance
* Free, open-source option
* Limited support for certain integrations and features

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, and are willing to pay for these conveniences. It's particularly suited for small to medium-sized teams that don't require advanced customization or control over their data. On the other hand, Mattermost is ideal for teams that value data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customizing their platform. This includes large enterprises or organizations with strict compliance requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure the necessary plugins and integrations.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a compatible import tool.
4. Test and verify that all data and functionality have been successfully migrated.
5. Update any existing workflows or integrations to work with Mattermost.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a robust and customizable solution for team collaboration. However, one technical limitation to consider is Mattermost's limited support for certain integrations, such as Google Drive or Trello, which may require additional setup or third-party plugins. Based on this comparison, we recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a team that values data ownership and security, and is willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customizing your platform.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like screen sharing or video conferencing
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that prioritize data ownership and security
* Large enterprises (over 100 users) with strict compliance requirements
* Teams that require custom plugins or integrations not available on Slack
* Organizations with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user fees

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost on my own server?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, allowing teams to maintain full control over their data and security.
### Is Mattermost compatible with all Slack integrations?
No, Mattermost has limited support for certain Slack integrations, and some may require additional setup or third-party plugins.
### How do I export my Slack data for migration to Mattermost?
You can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, open-source option for self-hosted teams.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Yes, Mattermost can be a good choice for small teams that prioritize data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customizing their platform.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being secure and customizable communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and hosting.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Element provides full data ownership, whereas Discord stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting, while Discord is easier to set up.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, especially when self-hosted, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary infrastructure.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (Nitro plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (Nitro plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Discord:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community and user base
* Robust features for gaming and community building
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data and hosting
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Full data ownership and control
* Highly customizable and scalable
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Requires technical expertise for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams, gaming communities, and individuals who prioritize ease of use and a large user base. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for organizations and teams that require high security, customizability, and control over their data, such as enterprises, governments, and open-source projects.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Import your exported data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any additional features, such as bridges or integrations.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its steep learning curve and technical requirements. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's federation feature, which allows communication between different Element servers, can be complex to set up and manage. We recommend switching to Element if you prioritize data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted server.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced features like screen sharing or video conferencing
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who require high security and customizability
* Enterprises with existing IT infrastructure and expertise
* Open-source projects that prioritize data ownership and control
* Individuals who value privacy and security above ease of use

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element is not directly compatible with Discord, but you can use bridges or integrations to connect the two platforms.
### Does Element support video conferencing?
Yes, Element supports video conferencing through its integration with Jitsi.
### Can I import my Discord data into Element?
Yes, you can import your Discord data into Element using the Element import tool.
### Is Element suitable for gaming communities?
No, Element is not yet suitable for gaming communities due to its limited support for gaming-specific features like screen sharing and low-latency voice chat.

# Notion vs AppFlowy (2026)

## Overview
Notion and AppFlowy are two popular tools used for note-taking, project management, and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from Notion to AppFlowy, particularly those seeking a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. * Data ownership: AppFlowy allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control over their information, whereas Notion stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Notion has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while AppFlowy requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: AppFlowy is designed to be highly scalable, making it a better choice for large teams, whereas Notion's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration: Notion has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party apps, while AppFlowy has a more limited set of integrations, but is open to community development.

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |

	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Extensive library of integrations
	+ Scalable for small to medium-sized teams
	+ Reliable customer support
	+ Constantly updated with new features
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Proprietary architecture limits customization
### AppFlowy
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full data control

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

* Small teams of 10-20 users who don't need Notion's collaborative features and want to reduce costs.
* Medium-sized teams of 50-100 users who need more control over their data and scalability.
* Large teams or organizations with over 200 users who require a high degree of customization and data ownership.
* Users who need advanced writing and formatting capabilities, such as support for markdown and LaTeX.
* Teams who don't need Notion's customer support and are comfortable with self-hosting and technical setup.

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Logseq?
Yes, Logseq can be self-hosted, giving users full control over their data and storage.
### Is Logseq free?
Yes, Logseq is free and open-source, with no costs per user.
### Can I import my Notion data into Logseq?
Yes, Logseq provides an import tool that supports importing data from Notion in CSV or JSON format.
### Does Logseq have a mobile app?
Logseq's mobile app is still in development, and users may experience some limitations when accessing their data on-the-go.
### Is Logseq suitable for small teams?
While Logseq can be used by small teams, it may be overkill for teams with simple needs, and Notion may be a better option.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular Git repository management tools used for version control and collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is to manage and track changes to code, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while Gitea is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: GitHub stores user data on its servers, while Gitea allows users to self-host and maintain control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while Gitea requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: GitHub has better scalability and support for large teams, while Gitea is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Feature Difference: GitHub has a more comprehensive project management feature set, including integrated issue tracking and project boards, while Gitea relies on third-party integrations for these features.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Comprehensive feature set, including integrated issue tracking and project boards
* Large community and support resources
* Scalable and reliable
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools and services
* Limited control over data and customization options
* Can be expensive for large teams
* Limited self-hosting options
* Proprietary license

**Gitea:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting options for complete control over data
* Customizable and extensible
* Lightweight and resource-efficient
* Growing community and support resources
* Limited scalability and support for large teams
* More complex setup process
* Limited integrated feature set, relying on third-party integrations
* May require additional technical expertise to maintain and customize

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for large teams, enterprises, and organizations that require a comprehensive feature set, scalability, and reliability. It is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem and want to take advantage of its integrations and support resources. On the other hand, Gitea is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, and organizations that value control over their data, customization options, and cost-effectiveness. It is also suitable for teams that are looking for a lightweight and resource-efficient solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which generates a `.git` archive file.
2. Set up a Gitea instance on your own server or use a hosted service.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to import your GitHub repository archive.
4. Configure your Gitea instance to match your GitHub setup, including user accounts, permissions, and integrations.
5. Test your Gitea instance to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a free and open-source solution with self-hosting options. However, it is essential to note that Gitea may not be suitable for very large teams or organizations that require a comprehensive feature set and scalability. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Gitea relies on third-party integrations for some features, which may require additional setup and maintenance. Overall, we recommend Gitea for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, and organizations that value control over their data and cost-effectiveness, while GitHub remains a better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a comprehensive feature set and scalability.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need integrated issue tracking and project boards
* Individuals who want control over their data and customization options
* Organizations with limited budgets that want to reduce costs
* Teams that value open-source and self-hosting options
* Developers who want a lightweight and resource-efficient solution

## FAQ
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is completely free and open-source. It can be self-hosted on your own server, and there are no per-user costs.

### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool and import it into Gitea using the Gitea import tool.

### Is Gitea suitable for large teams?
No, Gitea is not suitable for very large teams or organizations that require a comprehensive feature set and scalability. It is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.

### Does Gitea have integrated issue tracking and project boards?
No, Gitea relies on third-party integrations for issue tracking and project boards, whereas GitHub has these features integrated.

### Can I use Gitea with my existing GitHub account?
No, Gitea requires a separate account and setup process. However, you can import your GitHub repository into Gitea and use it as a replacement.

Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by designers, developers, and teams to create user interfaces, websites, and applications. * Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Figma stores design data on its proprietary servers, while Penpot allows users to self-host their designs.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up and configure.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex designs, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.

|--------|----------|---------|
